title: Theseus
titleEn: Theseus and the Poisoned Cup — Metamorphoses VII.404–452
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Theseus arrives unrecognised by his own father, and Medea mixes for his destruction an aconite she had once carried from the shores of Scythia — a poison these lines trace back to the foam of Cerberus, dragged up out of the dark by the hero of Tiryns. Aegeus himself holds out the cup, then makes out the marks of his own line on the ivory hilt of his son's sword and strikes the cup away; Medea escapes in a mist raised by her spells. The city then keeps festival, and a song over the wine counts up the road Theseus has cleared, from the bull at Marathon to the bones of Sciron hardened into cliffs.

sentences.t:
Iamque aderat Theseus, proles ignara parenti,
et virtute sua bimarem pacaverat Isthmon.
sentences.l: And now Theseus was at hand, offspring unknown to his parent, and by his own valour he had made peaceful the two-sea'd Isthmus.
sentences.i: And now Theseus had come, a son his father did not know, and by his own courage he had brought peace to the Isthmus between the two seas.
sentences.n: ignara is passive in force here — 'not known', not 'not knowing' — with parenti a dative naming the person to whom he is unknown. bimarem, 'two-sea'd', describes the Isthmus of Corinth, a neck of land with open water on either side; pacaverat, 'had pacified', points ahead to the road-clearing that the song at 433–447 will list one killing at a time. Magnus prints et, making this a second main clause; some editions print qui, 'who had pacified'.

sentences.t:
Huius in exitium miscet Medea quod olim
attulerat secum Scythicis aconiton ab oris.
sentences.l: For his destruction Medea mixes what she had once brought with her from Scythian shores — aconite.
sentences.i: To destroy him Medea mixes the aconite she had once carried with her from the shores of Scythia.
sentences.n: in with the accusative is purpose here, 'for his destruction', not motion. miscet is a historic present, dropping the narrative out of the past tense and into the moment. The word the relative clause depends on, aconiton, sits inside that clause instead of before it — an ordinary Latin arrangement that English has to unpick; the Greek ending -on marks the plant-name as a borrowing.

sentences.t:
Illud Echidneae memorant e dentibus ortum
esse canis.
sentences.l: That, they relate, arose from the teeth of the Echidnean hound.
sentences.i: It sprang, so the story runs, from the teeth of Echidna's hound.
sentences.n: memorant governs an accusative and infinitive, illud ... ortum esse, 'they relate that it arose' — a construction that holds the claim at the distance of report rather than vouching for it. Echidneae ... canis is a genitive, 'of the Echidnean hound': the dog of the underworld, named from his mother Echidna. The next lines say who brought him up into the light.

sentences.t:
Specus est tenebroso caecus hiatu,
est via declivis,
sentences.l: There is a cave, sightless with its shadowy gaping mouth; there is a way sloping downward,
sentences.i: There is a cave, blind-dark at its shadowy mouth, and a path that runs steeply down,
sentences.n: caecus, 'blind', is said of the cave itself and not of anyone inside it: the dark makes it both unseeing and unseen. The two clauses are set down side by side with no connecting word — est ... est — so that the place arrives in the order the eye would meet it.

sentences.t:
per quam Tirynthius heros
restantem contraque diem radiosque micantes
obliquantem oculos nexis adamante catenis
Cerberon abstraxit;
sentences.l: by which the Tirynthian hero dragged Cerberus off — resisting, and turning his eyes aside against the daylight and the flashing beams — with chains bound with adamant;
sentences.i: and by it the hero of Tiryns hauled Cerberus up, the dog digging in his heels and twisting his eyes away from the daylight and its glittering rays, in chains of adamant;
sentences.n: Tirynthius heros, 'the hero of Tiryns', is Hercules, named from the town he was raised in; bringing the hound of the dead up into the world above was the last of the labours laid on him. restantem and obliquantem are present participles agreeing with Cerberon, holding the struggle in the present tense: the dog braces backwards while his eyes swerve from a light he has never seen. nexis adamante catenis is an ablative of means — 'with chains bound with adamant', the unbreakable metal of myth.

sentences.t:
rabida qui concitus ira
implevit pariter ternis latratibus auras
et sparsit virides spumis albentibus agros.
sentences.l: and he, stirred up by rabid rage, filled the airs all at once with threefold barking and sprinkled the green fields with whitening foam.
sentences.i: and he, roused to a rabid fury, filled the air with all three throats baying at once and spattered the green fields with white foam.
sentences.n: qui opens the sentence as a connecting relative — Latin's way of writing 'and he' without a new subject. ternis latratibus, 'with threefold barking', and pariter, 'equally, at one and the same time', give the picture together: three heads in one breath. The foam is not scene-painting; it is the ingredient the next lines make the poison from.

sentences.t:
Has concresse putant nactasque alimenta feracis
fecundique soli vires cepisse nocendi.
sentences.l: These, they think, hardened, and, having got nourishment from the teeming and fruitful soil, took on the strength of doing harm.
sentences.i: The foam, they believe, congealed, and, drawing nourishment from the rich and fertile ground, took on its power to poison.
sentences.n: concresse is a shortened form of concrevisse, the perfect infinitive — verse contracts these freely. putant carries two infinitives in a row, concresse and cepisse, both belonging to has, 'these' (the spatters of foam). nactas comes from the deponent nanciscor: passive in form, active in meaning, 'having obtained'. nocendi is a gerund in the genitive, 'of harming' — the plant's strength is a strength for doing harm.

sentences.t:
Quae quia nascuntur dura vivacia caute,
agrestes aconita vocant.
sentences.l: And because these, tenacious of life, are born upon hard crag, the country people call them aconites.
sentences.i: And because they spring up, hardy, on bare rock, country people call them aconites.
sentences.n: Quae is a connecting relative, 'and these'. The couplet is an explanation of the name: the ancients derived aconitum from a Greek word for a bare rock or whetstone, so dura caute — ablative, 'on hard crag' — is offered as the etymology. vivacia is 'long-lived, hard to kill'. It is the agrestes, the people who work the land, who do the naming, not the poets.

sentences.t:
Ea coniugis astu
ipse parens Aegeus nato porrexit ut hosti.
sentences.l: These, by the cunning of his wife, the parent himself, Aegeus, held out to his son as to an enemy.
sentences.i: These, at his wife's contriving, Aegeus the father held out with his own hand to his own son, as though to an enemy.
sentences.n: coniugis astu is an ablative of means, 'by the wife's cunning' — the noun for her is neutral and all the weight falls on astu. ipse parens, 'the parent himself', sharpens the horror: the father in person, not a servant. ut hosti is a dative in a comparison, 'as to an enemy' — he does exactly what he would do to a foe, and the whole point is that he does not know which of the two is standing in front of him.

sentences.t:
Sumpserat ignara Theseus data pocula dextra,
cum pater in capulo gladii cognovit eburno
signa sui generis facinusque excussit ab ore.
sentences.l: Theseus had taken up the proffered cup with unknowing right hand, when the father recognised on the ivory hilt of the sword the tokens of his own line and struck the crime away from his mouth.
sentences.i: Theseus had taken the offered cup in an unwitting hand when his father made out, on the sword's ivory hilt, the marks of his own blood — and dashed the crime from his son's lips.
sentences.n: ignara dextra is ablative, 'with unknowing right hand': the hand is called ignorant in place of the man, so that the whole danger sits in the gesture. The cum clause is the inverted kind, where the 'when' clause carries the turn of events and the main verb only sets the scene for it. facinus, 'the crime', is used for the cup itself — what Aegeus knocks away is not a drink but the deed it would have been.

sentences.t: Effugit illa necem nebulis per carmina motis.
sentences.l: She escaped her killing, with mists set moving by means of spells.
sentences.i: She escaped death, raising a mist by her incantations.
sentences.n: nebulis ... motis is an ablative absolute — a self-contained 'with X done' phrase where English wants a clause: 'once mists had been raised'. per carmina, 'through spells', names how. Ovid gives Medea's escape a single line and no more.

sentences.t:
At genitor, quamquam laetatur sospite nato,
attonitus tamen est ingens discrimine parvo
committi potuisse nefas.
sentences.l: But the father, although he rejoices with his son safe, is thunderstruck all the same that so vast an outrage could have been committed by so small a margin.
sentences.i: But the father, glad though he is that his son is safe, is stunned all the same that a horror so enormous had come so close to being done.
sentences.n: sospite nato is an ablative absolute, 'his son being safe', giving the ground of the joy. attonitus, 'thunderstruck', takes the accusative and infinitive that follows it: what stuns him is nefas ... committi potuisse, 'that an unspeakable act could have been committed'. ingens is held away from its own noun nefas across the line-end, with discrimine parvo set down between them — the enormity, and the hair's breadth.

sentences.t:
Fovet ignibus aras
muneribusque deos implet,
sentences.l: He keeps the altars warm with fires and fills the gods with offerings,
sentences.i: He keeps the fires alive on the altars and heaps the gods with offerings,
sentences.n: fovet is 'keeps warm, cherishes', the verb used of nursing something living; the altars are tended rather than merely lit. deos implet, 'fills the gods', is compressed — the same verb would serve for filling a jar, and the gifts are piled until the gods have their fill.

sentences.t:
feriuntque secures
colla torosa boum vinctorum corpora vittis.
sentences.l: and the axes strike the muscled necks of oxen bound as to their bodies with fillets.
sentences.i: and the axes come down on the thick necks of oxen with the sacred ribbons wound about them.
sentences.n: corpora is a Greek accusative of respect after vinctorum — 'bound as to their bodies' — a Greek turn that Latin verse borrows; plain English needs 'bound about the body'. The vittae are the woollen fillets tied on a victim to mark it as set apart for a god. Notice that secures, 'the axes', and not the men holding them, is made the subject. Magnus prints corpora, 'bodies'; some editions print cornua, 'horns', which puts the ribbons on the head instead.

sentences.t:
Nullus Erechthidis fertur celebratior illo
inluxisse dies.
sentences.l: No day is reported to have dawned for the sons of Erechtheus more thronged with festival than that one.
sentences.i: No day, they say, ever dawned on the children of Erechtheus more full of celebration than that.
sentences.n: Erechthidis is a dative plural, 'for the sons of Erechtheus': Erechtheus was an early king of Athens, and the patronymic simply means the Athenians. fertur ... inluxisse, 'is said to have dawned', keeps the claim at the distance of hearsay, as memorant did at the start of the poison's story. illo is an ablative of comparison after celebratior, 'more festive than that one'.

sentences.t:
Agitant convivia patres
et medium vulgus, nec non et carmina, vino
ingenium faciente, canunt:
sentences.l: The fathers keep up feasting, and the middling crowd too, and no less do they sing songs, with the wine making their wit:
sentences.i: The elders keep the banqueting going, and the common people with them, and they sing songs as well, the wine supplying the invention:
sentences.n: patres, 'the fathers', are the city's leading men, set against medium vulgus, 'the middle crowd', the ordinary people — high and low both, which is the point. nec non et is a doubled negative used as an emphatic 'and also'. vino ingenium faciente is an ablative absolute, 'with wine making the talent' — a dry aside on where the poetry that follows comes from.

sentences.t:
“Te, maxime Theseu,
mirata est Marathon Cretaei sanguine tauri;
sentences.l: “You, greatest Theseus, Marathon marvelled at, for the blood of the Cretan bull;
sentences.i: “You, mightiest Theseus, Marathon gazed on in wonder, for the blood of the Cretan bull;
sentences.n: The song turns and speaks to Theseus directly — te, 'you' — and keeps the second person to its last word. mirata est is from the deponent miror: passive in form, active in sense, 'she wondered at'. Marathon, the plain north-east of Athens, is made the one who wonders, the place standing in for the people who saw it; sanguine is an ablative of cause, the blood being what the wonder was for.

sentences.t:
quodque suis securus arat Cromyona colonus,
munus opusque tuum est.
sentences.l: and that the farmer ploughs Cromyon untroubled with his own team, that is your gift and your work.
sentences.i: and that the farmer at Cromyon ploughs with his own oxen and fears nothing — that is your gift and your doing.
sentences.n: The whole clause quod ... arat, 'the fact that he ploughs', is the subject of est: 'that he ploughs is your gift'. securus is 'free from care', a man working unafraid. suis is an ablative with its noun left out, 'with his own', understood of the plough-team. Cromyon lies on the Isthmus road; what the ploughman there no longer has to fear the song does not trouble to name.

sentences.t:
Tellus Epidauria per te
clavigeram vidit Vulcani occumbere prolem,
sentences.l: The Epidaurian land, through you, saw the club-bearing offspring of Vulcan go down,
sentences.i: The land of Epidaurus saw, by your doing, the club-bearing son of Vulcan fall,
sentences.n: vidit takes an accusative and infinitive, prolem ... occumbere, 'saw the offspring go down'. clavigeram, 'club-bearing', is a compound adjective of the sort Latin verse builds freely, and it identifies the man by his weapon instead of his name. per te, 'through you', gives Theseus the deed while leaving the land as the eye that watched it.

sentences.t: vidit et inmitem Cephisias ora Procrusten,
sentences.l: and the Cephisian bank saw pitiless Procrustes go down too,
sentences.i: the bank of the Cephisus saw pitiless Procrustes go the same way,
sentences.n: The verb repeats and the infinitive occumbere from the line before has to be carried over: 'saw Procrustes fall too'. Cephisias ora is 'the Cephisian shore', the bank of the river that runs past Athens. inmitem, 'unsoftened, pitiless', is the song's whole verdict on the man; what he did to travellers is left unsaid.

sentences.t: Cercyonis letum vidit Cerealis Eleusin.
sentences.l: the death of Cercyon, Eleusis of Ceres saw.
sentences.i: and Eleusis, the town of Ceres, saw Cercyon die.
sentences.n: Three clauses running are built on vidit, each with a different place as the eye — a piling-up that turns the road itself into the witness. Eleusin, 'Eleusis', keeps its Greek shape but stands as the subject; the town lies west of Athens and was the seat of Ceres' mysteries, which is why Cerealis is attached to it. letum is the flat word for a death, carrying none of the ceremony of the place.

sentences.t:
Occidit ille Sinis, magnis male viribus usus,
qui poterat curvare trabes et agebat ab alto
ad terram late sparsuras corpora pinus.
sentences.l: That Sinis fell, having used his great strength badly, who could bend tree-trunks and used to drag down from on high to the ground pines about to scatter bodies far and wide.
sentences.i: Sinis fell, who put his great strength to bad use — he could bend whole trunks, and would haul pines down from their height to the ground to fling men's bodies wide.
sentences.n: usus is from the deponent utor, active in sense and governing the ablative viribus: 'having used his strength'. male, 'badly', is the entire charge against him, set in one word between magnis and viribus. sparsuras is a future participle agreeing with pinus, 'pines about to scatter' — it folds the outcome into the description of the trees, so the reader sees what the bent pine is for before being told what it did.

sentences.t:
Tutus ad Alcathoen, Lelegeia moenia, limes
composito Scirone patet,
sentences.l: With Sciron settled, a safe track lies open to Alcathoe, the Lelegeian walls,
sentences.i: Now that Sciron is disposed of, the road to Alcathoe — the Lelegeian city — lies open and safe,
sentences.n: composito Scirone is an ablative absolute, 'Sciron having been settled'. componere is a mild, tidy word — to arrange, to lay out, and it can be used of laying a body to rest; the song reaches for it rather than for any word meaning 'killed'. Alcathoe is Megara, named from its builder Alcathous, and Lelegeia moenia, 'the Lelegeian walls', stands in apposition to it, the Leleges being reckoned an old people of that coast.

sentences.t:
sparsisque latronis
terra negat sedem, sedem negat ossibus unda;
sentences.l: and to the scattered bones of the brigand the earth denies a resting-place, a resting-place the water denies the bones;
sentences.i: and the earth grants the scattered bones of the robber no resting-place, and no resting-place does the sea grant them either;
sentences.n: negat takes a dative of the one refused and an accusative of the thing refused: 'denies a seat to the bones'. The two halves of the line are turned back to front against each other — terra negat sedem, sedem negat ... unda — so that earth and water close round the bones with no gap between them. latronis, 'of the brigand', is the song's name for him and carries its contempt openly.

sentences.t:
quae iactata diu fertur durasse vetustas
in scopulos: scopulis nomen Scironis inhaeret.
sentences.l: and these, long tossed about, great age is said to have hardened into crags: to the crags the name of Sciron clings.
sentences.i: and age, they say, hardened them, after long tossing, into cliffs: to those cliffs the name of Sciron still clings.
sentences.n: quae is a connecting relative picking up the bones, 'and these'. vetustas, 'great age', is the subject and durasse — a contracted form of duravisse — is transitive here, 'to have hardened them'; fertur once more keeps it a matter of report. The handing-on of scopulos to scopulis across the colon is the hinge of the aetiology: the Scironian rocks on that coast road carry his name.

sentences.t:
Si titulos annosque tuos numerare velimus,
facta premant annos.
sentences.l: If we should wish to count up your titles and your years, your deeds would press down your years.
sentences.i: If we cared to count your honours and your years, the deeds would outweigh the years.
sentences.n: velimus and premant are both present subjunctives — the 'should ... would' condition, which puts the reckoning forward as merely imagined rather than done. titulos are the honours a name carries; the compliment is that a young man's list of deeds already runs longer than his list of years. Magnus prints premant, the subjunctive; some editions print prement, a plain future, 'will outweigh'.

sentences.t:
Pro te, fortissime, vota
publica suscipimus, Bacchi tibi sumimus haustus.”
sentences.l: On your behalf, bravest one, we take up public vows; draughts of Bacchus we take up for you.”
sentences.i: For you, bravest of men, we undertake the vows of the whole people; for you we lift our cups of Bacchus.”
sentences.n: vota suscipere is the settled phrase for formally undertaking a vow to the gods, and publica makes it the city's act and not a private one. Bacchi ... haustus, 'draughts of Bacchus', names the god where the wine is meant, a figure Latin uses constantly. suscipimus and sumimus are set close for the sound of them: the vow and the cup taken up in one motion.

sentences.t:
Consonat adsensu populi precibusque faventum
regia, nec tota tristis locus ullus in urbe est.
sentences.l: The palace sounds together with the assent of the people and the prayers of those favouring him, nor is any place in the whole city downcast.
sentences.i: The palace rings with the people's assent and the prayers of well-wishers, and in the whole city there is not one place that is sad.
sentences.n: Consonat, 'sounds together', stands first and its subject regia, 'the palace', is held back to the opening of the next line — the noise reaches the reader before the building does. faventum is the genitive plural of the participle of faveo, 'those showing favour', the word used of a crowd's goodwill at a public occasion. The last line states the city's gladness by denying its opposite, which leaves the sadness faintly in the air.
